facts.claim: DelegationData has seven plain Field members: delegatorWalletId, delegateWalletId, scopeFlags, effectiveDate, expirationDate, relationshipCode and delegationHash. commitment() is the Poseidon hash of all seven in that order, with no salt or blinding factor. Anyone who knows or can guess the two wallet IDs and the small-domain fields can recompute a leaf.

Scope flags are READ=1, WRITE=2, PICKUP=4 and MESSAGING=8. SCOPE_ALL=7 leaves MESSAGING out. Relationship codes are 1 Parent, 2 Spouse, 3 POA, 4 Guardian, 5 Migration and 6 Appointed Rep. There is no code for grandparent, sibling, aunt/uncle or other kin, and no field for depth, sub-delegation or on-behalf-of.

Dates are raw CCYYMMDD numbers (dateToField = Field(BigInt(str))), not hashed. In the library, delegationHash = hashString(legalDocumentRef). In AOR it is buildAorCommitment. In the running engine's createDelegation it is hashString(`DEL-${Date.now()}`), which binds to no document.

DelegationRegistry: DELEGATION_TREE_HEIGHT=8, so at most 128 delegations for the whole network. Each leaf is DelegationData.commitment(). The class keeps a plaintext Map from index to the full DelegationData. revokeDelegation sets the leaf to Field(0) and the slot is never reused. findByWallets is a linear scan comparing plaintext wallet IDs. getWitness returns DelegationRegistryWitness (MerkleWitness(8)).

The delegation root exists only in engine memory. A comment says it is packed into CareContract slot 7, but CareContract is never compiled or deployed. The engine computes messagingRoot only for getChainState. The sequencer's adminState.messagingRoot can only be set through setAdminState, and grep found no caller. Unlike sendMessage, createDelegation does not call emitMessagingAuditEvent, so the sequencer never sees a delegation.
Delegations are not persisted. AdjudicationCheckpointState has no delegation field, and the registry is built empty at engine start, so a restart loses every delegation.

getState() lists every delegation with delegator and delegate wallet IDs, scopeFlags and relationshipCode in the clear. /interactive/state is in ADMIN_ROUTES and in no node role's allow-list, so only the operator can read it.

MessagingProgram has no publicInput, only publicOutput MessagingOutput. proveDelegate takes six private inputs: DelegationData, DelegationRegistryWitness, messageRegistryRoot, delegationRegistryRoot, keyRegistryRoot and currentDate. It asserts four things: the commitment is in the tree; messagingRoot = Poseidon(msgRoot, delRoot, keyRoot); effectiveDate <= currentDate <= expirationDate; scopeFlags > 0.

The current delegation proof makes the relationship code public. MessagingOutput.messageType = relationshipCode, senderWalletId = delegator, recipientWalletId = delegate, contentHash = scopeFlags, plus the commitment, operationType=2 and messagingRoot.

proveDelegate has five gaps. currentDate is a private input the prover chooses, so the expiry check is self-attested (the engine passes a hard-coded '20260214'). Nothing proves the prover controls the delegate wallet. The PICKUP bit is not checked specifically. There is no challenge, nullifier or binding to a prescription. The engine discards the generated proof.

createDelegation requires both wallets to be in enrolledMembers and different from each other. It does not range-check scopeFlags or relationshipCode; the route checks only typeof number. Effective and expiry dates are hard-coded (20260214 / 20270214). It inserts the leaf, then proves. It emits a viz event with both display names and the scope labels but not the relationship. It returns relationshipCode and relationshipLabel to the caller.

createDelegation writes the console lines '═══ Delegation: <delegator name> → <delegate name> ═══' and 'Relationship: <label>'. The console emitter prints them to server stdout and broadcasts them on the SSE stream GET /interactive/console. That path is in neither ADMIN_ROUTES nor GATED_READS, so reg() registers it without the admin gate. The relationship label and the names leak to logs and to any console subscriber.
POST /interactive/create-delegation is in ADMIN_ROUTES and in no role's ROUTES_BY_ROLE, so only the operator can call it. No member-device or wallet-signed route can create or revoke a delegation.

AOR constants: message types AOR_INITIATE 10 to AOR_DATA_SHARE 17; PICKUP_COOLDOWN_MS 48 h; AOR validity 365 days; rate limit 24 h; RepEnrollmentToken expiry 24 h; OFFLINE_TTL_MS READ 72 h, WRITE 24 h, PICKUP 4 h.

AorLocalData is the full CMS-1696 form: party name, identifier, address, phone, signature and dates, plus the representative's name, 'repProfessionalStatus' ('Professional status or relationship to party'), fee and liability waivers. buildAorCommitment hashes six of these fields with unsalted hashString/dateToField: party name, party identifier, rep name, rep status/relationship and both signing dates. These are low-entropy inputs, so the commitment can be dictionary-inverted the way finding A-1 inverted the unsalted wallet hashes.

Two-message confirmation: the member sends AOR_INITIATE and then AOR_CONFIRMED. The CONFIRMED contentHash = Poseidon(memberWalletId, repWalletId, aorCommitment, scopeFlags). These are ordinary messages, and the sequencer stores message metadata (senderWalletId, recipientWalletId, messageType) in the clear. The AOR flow therefore exposes the member-to-rep link, and the AOR message types make the relationship visible.

AorService.buildDelegation always sets relationshipCode = 6 (Appointed Rep). isPickupEligible is off-circuit JavaScript. It checks the PICKUP bit and expiry, and enforces the cool-down as effectiveDate at midnight UTC plus 48 h. The cool-down therefore runs from the self-declared effective date, not from when the leaf was inserted, and a back-dated effectiveDate skips it.

isOfflineCredentialValid applies the TTL of the highest scope requested to the pharmacy's chain-state staleness. revokeAor accepts the revoker if its wallet ID string equals the member's or the admin's, with no signature or proof. It looks the leaf up by the wallet pair, refuses a code other than 6, and zeroes the leaf. isDelegationActive is a Map lookup. AorService is static and stateless, and the running network never calls it; only tests/aor.test.ts and the src/index.ts exports reference it.

PortableDelegationCredential carries the full DelegationData in the clear: both wallet IDs, scope, dates, relationshipCode and delegationHash. It also carries delegationIndex, the Merkle witnessPath and witnessIsLefts, delegationRegistryRoot, messagingRoot, chainStateTimestamp and createdAt. It has no proof, no signature and no holder binding. Only serialize and deserialize exist; there is no verifier function anywhere in the codebase.
verifyCredentialOffline (for the non-delegation PortableCredential) ignores its verificationKey argument and calls CredentialProgram.verify(proof) using the in-process compiled program.

ProofGateProgram's only public input is the wallet ID. verifyRepresentative asserts Poseidon(3, qualifierCode, representativeIdHash, enrollmentKeyHash) == walletIdentity. No challenge or nonce enters any ProofGate proof, so an ownership proof can be replayed and binds to no session or prescription.

Domain tags: MEMBER 0, PRESCRIBER 1, PHARMACY 2, REPRESENTATIVE 3. deriveRepresentativeWalletId = Poseidon(3, qualifier, hashString(representativeId), hashString(enrollmentKey)). representativeId (driver licence, state ID, bar number or org ID) is hashed without salt, unlike the member derivation, which salts identity fields per member.

RepEnrollmentToken holds tokenIdHash, memberWalletId (the authorizing member, in the clear), scopeFlags, validUntil, issuerHash and nonce, and the insurer issues it. No route enrolls a representative: grep finds no use of RepEnrollmentToken, deriveRepresentativeWalletId or verifyRepresentative under src/nodes, src/adjudication or src/l2. secureRepresentativeDerivation exists only as a library function.

The prescriber names the patient only by memberWalletId. The prescriber node's POST /prescriptions/write and /prescriptions/prescribe take memberWalletId, pharmacyWalletId and ndcHash (plus brandName, quantity, daysSupply, refills, directions, diagnosis). No field says the patient is a dependent or names a guardian or delegate.

The eScript JSON, which includes memberWalletId and diagnosis, is E2E-encrypted (X25519 + AES-GCM) separately for the pharmacy and for the member. Both copies are stored on the sequencer with senderWalletId, recipientWalletId and messageType '3', and they share one threadIdHash = hashString(`rx-${rxId}`) and one messageCommitment. Any extra copy to a delegate would link that delegate to the patient in sequencer metadata.

After sending the eScript, the prescriber node calls the engine's POST /interactive/prescribe with {prescriberIndex, memberWalletId, ndcHash, pharmacyIndex, quantity, refills, rxId}. The prescriber role is allowed to call it.

Consent (B5): for a member with a device, createPrescription refuses with 403 unless the prescriber is the member's consented PCP or holds a live authorization from the member's device. That authorization is wallet-signed through the member route /authorizations/prescriber to /interactive/prescriber-authorization, lasts 1-72 h and can be limited to one NDC. The PCP assignment is wallet-signed too. Only the patient's own wallet key can grant either, so a dependent without a device cannot consent and no guardian path exists.
A device holds one wallet: NautilusStateData has a single walletId, enrollmentKey, preimageFields and domainTag.

PrescriptionData has ndcHash, prescriberWalletId, memberWalletId, writtenDate, expirationDate, quantityPrescribed and refillsAuthorized. commitment() is their unsalted Poseidon hash, which is the rxCommitment. The engine's PrescriptionState adds memberWalletId, ndcHash, prescriber and pharmacy indices, quantities, refills, status and history.

The pharmacy's POST /dispensing/dispense takes {prescriptionId, quantityDispensed, ingredientCostCents, dispensingFeeCents}, checks only that prescriptionId is present, and forwards to the engine's /interactive/fill. dispensePrescription checks that the prescription exists and is FILLED or PARTIALLY_FILLED, that the member is not REVOKED, the quantity, and the D4 duplicate key. Its comment reads 'No credential needed — fills are reversible', and credentialJson is optional and unused. Nobody checks who is at the counter.

The pharmacy dashboard enables Dispense only in the browser, and only when a verified attestation's wallet equals the claim's memberWalletId. A delegate presenting their own attestation would be refused, and the server enforces nothing.

/nfc/scan verifies an attestation against the pinned sequencer key when one is supplied. It also accepts a bare walletId with no verification (priority 4). Either way it returns that wallet's active medications and full drug history.

NfcCredentialAttestation contains v, t, w (wallet ID in the clear), cc, ls (lifecycle), fr, ts, exp, n (revocation nonce), pk and sig. The signed message is 'zkpcare-attestation-v2|w|cc|ls|fr|ts|exp|n' and the default lifetime is 24 h. The file states that nothing on the tag is secret and that the nonce is not an authentication factor, so the attestation is a bearer token. verifyAttestation checks the pinned key, the signature and expiry. The revocation set lives only in the issuer, and /nfc/scan does not consult it.

The sequencer issues attestations to callers that sign as the wallet (l2-node requestAttestation). It sets credentialCommitment to the registry root ('Best available commitment') and refuses revoked wallets. The engine's credential-generation path also creates one.

Family binding (B8/A-34, uncommitted): MemberApproval.familyIdHash comes from the insurer. approveMember refuses a second approval with a different group, plan or family. registerMemberFromEnrollment sets familyId = approval.familyIdHash and relationship = the device-reported opts.relationship || 'SELF', which is display only. familyMembersOf pools members with the same familyId, groupId and planId. familyLimitsFor returns zero limits when there is no family or no plan.

getFamilyHistory returns each family member's display name, truncated walletIdStr, relationship label and accumulators. The insurer role may call GET /interactive/family-history, so the insurer sees family composition and the relationship labels.

The employer node's TokenAuthority computes and stores the exact familyIdHash the engine later binds: hashString of the HR Tool's seeded hash hashFamilyId(familyId, groupSeed). The HR roster's required columns are employee_id, family_id, first_name, last_name and dob; there is no relationship column. src/l2 has no family concept.

No nullifier exists anywhere in src (grep -i nullifier: 0 hits). Existing replay protection covers other things: the sequencer's proof fingerprint on registry and lifecycle transitions, the D4 duplicate-fill key, and the HTTP signed-request ReplayCache.

Reusable primitives. ForestDomain: MEMBER 0, PRESCRIBER 1, PHARMACY 2, MEDICATION 3, ACCESS_CONTROL 4, TRANSACTION 5, each tree height 8. CredentialData: credentialType (ELIGIBILITY=1, PRESCRIPTION=2), forestRoot, issuer, subject wallet, issuedAt, expiresAt, revoked. CredentialProgram.proveMint, proveHolding and proveHoldingByType all output walletId and credentialCommitment publicly.

Each wallet has an Ed25519 signing key and an X25519 encryption key, both derived from the enrollment key by HKDF; the public halves are registered on the sequencer. l2_getEncryptionKey answers signed callers. KeyRegistry height is 11. Message type '7' access_grant is mapped in the RPC server, but nothing sends it.

The hardening plan already leans this way. Delegated pickup 'belongs' on the domain-tag-3 representative mechanism 'with its own authorization rather than by sharing a card'. Pending owner decision (3) recommends 'a representative pickup flag the member sets on the device for a named person and a window, and no card-only pickup otherwise'. B3 makes the member's offline attestation at pickup the finalize step.
The code has no concept of age or minor status (grep for minor/age checks: 0 hits), and the date of birth is salted inside the wallet preimage.

implications: Interpretation (a), kinship degree: the network has no source that can verify kinship. relationshipCode is whatever the grantor asserts, the HR roster has only family_id, and the B8 family hash proves only co-coverage in one group and plan. Grandparents, aunts and siblings are usually not on the plan at all. So the pharmacy should check authorization to receive this prescription, never a kinship degree. If kinship is kept for audit or dispute, it goes into the leaf as a salted committed field and never into a public output.

Interpretation (b), authority through an intermediary: model it as a chain of grants, not a relationship graph. Option 1 (recommended, simplest circuit): flatten at issuance. The guardian's device issues a leaf naming the patient (the child's wallet) and the delegate (the grandparent's commitment), and proves its guardian authority in the issuance proof. The pickup proof then checks one leaf and never learns there was an intermediary. Option 2: a two-leaf or recursive proof with a parentLeaf link and a canSubdelegate/maxDepth flag, so the pickup proof checks patient<-guardian and guardian<-delegate privately. Option 2 needs both new fields, which DelegationData lacks today.

Replace the leaf with a hiding commitment, e.g. Poseidon(salt, patientWalletId, delegateCommitment, scopeFlags, notBefore, notAfter, relationshipCode, parentLeaf/depth, docHash). The engine or sequencer stores only the leaf; the opening lives on the grantor's and delegate's devices. Today the engine keeps a plaintext Map of DelegationData, lists it in getState, and logs the relationship label, so all three must change.

A new pickup circuit is needed. The existing proveDelegate makes both wallet IDs and the relationship code public, self-attests the date, and has no holder binding. Public inputs: delegationRoot, an rx binding (PrescriptionData.commitment() or a prescriptionId hash), a fresh pharmacy challenge, and the verifier-supplied date. Private inputs: the leaf opening, Merkle witness(es), and the delegate's ProofGate-style preimage, proving knowledge of the secret behind the delegate wallet or commitment. Assertions: leaf in root, PICKUP bit set, dates valid, patient == rx.memberWalletId. Public output: rx binding, challenge, nullifier = Poseidon(delegateSecret, rxId, fillNumber), and root. The relationship code and the delegate's wallet never appear.

Holder binding: the NFC attestation is a bearer token and ProofGate proofs carry no challenge. A card-only or attestation-only pickup therefore proves possession, not authorization, which is the point plan §7 makes. The pickup proof must be made on the delegate's device over a pharmacy-issued nonce.

Revocation and freshness need a published root. Today the delegation root lives only in engine memory, is never sent to the sequencer, and is lost on restart. The PICKUP 4 h offline TTL only works if the pharmacy can fetch a root no older than 4 h, so the root needs a sequencer-recorded slot with an audit event. The 48 h cool-down should be measured from the sequencer-recorded insertion time, not the self-declared effectiveDate.
Capacity: a delegation tree of height 8 holds 128 leaves for the whole network. Production needs a much taller tree (e.g. height 20) or partitioning.

Delegate identity: a delegate who is not a member, such as a grandparent off the plan, needs either a representative wallet (domain tag 3, with no enrollment route today) or an anonymous one-time pickup secret generated by the guardian's device per prescription and shared out of band (QR). The secret approach avoids enrolling the delegate at all and gives the strongest unlinkability. RepEnrollmentToken carries memberWalletId in the clear, so it would need to carry a commitment instead.

The prescriber should name only the patient (the dependent's wallet) and never learn the guardian or delegate. Consent for a dependent without a device needs a guardian path in createPrescription, next to B5's PCP and device-authorization checks. That path would accept a wallet-signed or ZK statement 'holder of a guardian/parent leaf for patient W authorizes prescriber P (optionally NDC N) until T'. Today only the patient's own wallet key can consent.

Dependents' wallets: one wallet per device means a child without a phone has no wallet, no consent path and no X25519 key to receive the eScript. Either support several wallets on one device (custodial dependent wallets held by the guardian), or give the dependent its own card or device. The owner's idea of putting family members into the enrollment hash would change wallet IDs on every life event. It would also break approveMember's immutable family binding, the per-person accumulators, the PA records and any delegation leaf keyed by wallet. Per-person wallets plus revocable delegation leaves avoid that.

Do not use familyIdHash as a public delegation anchor. The employer node holds the identical value, so publishing it next to wallets would let the employer link families to wallets (I6). The engine already holds it per wallet, and the insurer sees relationship labels through family-history.

Metadata to keep off the network: shared threadIdHash and messageCommitment on per-recipient eScript copies; AOR message types 10-17, which announce the relation; the console 'Relationship:' line on an ungated SSE stream; viz events naming the delegator and delegate. The 'ready for pickup' notice to a delegate should be forwarded E2E by the patient's or guardian's device, or sent on an unlinkable per-recipient thread, not as a prescriber-to-delegate eScript.

The counter must enforce pickup on the server. /dispensing/dispense (and the B3 finalize) should require either the patient's attestation or a verified pickup proof bound to that prescriptionId, with the nullifier recorded to prevent double pickup and to leave an audit handle. The dashboard's wallet-equality gate would block delegates, and the bare-walletId history lookup on /nfc/scan should not be part of a delegated pickup.

AOR (CMS-1696) is an appeals and representation instrument and heavier than family pickup needs. Its cool-down, TTL tiers and revocation ideas are reusable. Its unsalted document commitment and clear-text message types are not.
open_questions: Does the owner want kinship degree verified at all, or only that the person is authorized to pick up? And who is the source of truth for a guardian-to-child relationship: the employer roster (family_id only), the insurer at enrollment, or a legal document (guardianship or POA) committed as docHash?

Does any state pharmacy rule the network must support require the pharmacist to record the pickup person's ID or relationship (for example for controlled substances, which release one excludes)? If so, where may that record live without breaking I1/I2: only at the pharmacy?

Will dependents (children) get their own wallet? On which device: a custodial second wallet on the guardian's phone, a card, or their own phone? How is age-out at 18 handled when the date of birth is salted in the preimage and there is no age concept?

Should the delegate be an enrolled member, a representative wallet (domain tag 3, which needs an enrollment route), or an unenrolled holder of a one-time per-prescription pickup secret from the guardian's device?
Flatten at issuance (one leaf, simplest circuit), or keep explicit multi-hop chains with sub-delegation? If chains, what is the maximum depth, and may a delegate re-delegate?
Where is the delegation root published and who signs updates: a new sequencer slot or RPC, the dormant adminState.messagingRoot, or a ChainProgram field? What audit event goes with it?
Does the 48 h pickup cool-down apply to guardian-issued family grants (a sick child may need same-day pickup), or only to AOR and representative grants?
Should the prescriber learn that a guardian consented for a minor, and must that consent be revealed or only proven in ZK?
How does the pickup proof fit B3's adjudicate-then-finalize: does a delegate's proof finalize the pending settlement exactly like the member's attestation, and who carries the accumulator witness?
Mail order (no counter moment): does the delegation model need a pre-authorized finalize bound to a delivery window?

facts.claim: HIPAA 45 CFR 164.510(b)(1)(i) lets a covered entity disclose PHI 'directly relevant to such person's involvement' in care or payment to 'a family member, other relative, or a close personal friend of the individual, or any other person identified by the individual'. Kinship degree plays no part. A person the patient names is enough.

45 CFR 164.510(b)(3) explicitly lets a covered entity 'use professional judgment and its experience with common practice to make reasonable inferences' about the individual's best interest in allowing a person to act on the individual's behalf 'to pick up filled prescriptions, medical supplies, X-rays, or other similar forms of protected health information'.

HHS FAQs 263 and 535: a relative or friend who arrives at a pharmacy and asks for a specific prescription is treated as involved in the patient's care, and the pharmacist may hand over the filled prescription. The patient does not need to give the pharmacist names in advance.

HIPAA's verification rule, 164.514(h)(1)(i), requires checking a requester's identity and authority 'except with respect to disclosures under § 164.510'. Under (h)(2)(iv), relying on professional judgment for a 164.510 disclosure satisfies verification. Disclosures to a personal representative are not exempt, so that person's authority must be verified.

Personal representatives (164.502(g)(1)-(2)): a personal representative is treated as the individual. For an adult or emancipated minor, the personal representative is a person with legal authority to make health care decisions: a health care POA, a court-appointed guardian, or a general or durable POA that includes health care powers. HHS: where authority is limited (for example, a POA covering only life support), the person is a representative only for PHI relevant to that authority.
facts.source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.502 ; HHS 'Guidance: Personal Representatives' (https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/personal-representatives/index.html, archived copy at https://www.sog.unc.edu/sites/www.sog.unc.edu/files/Guidance_%20Personal%20Representatives%20_%20HHS.gov_.pdf)

facts.claim: For an unemancipated minor, a parent, guardian or person in loco parentis is the personal representative, except where (A) the minor consents to a service for which state law requires no other consent, (B) the minor may lawfully obtain the service without parental consent and the minor, a court or another authorized person consents, or (C) the parent agreed to a confidentiality agreement between the provider and the minor. Under 164.502(g)(3)(ii), state law that permits, requires or prohibits disclosure to parents controls. Where state law is silent and an exception applies, a licensed professional decides using professional judgment.
facts.source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.502 ; HHS personal representatives guidance (UNC archived PDF above)

facts.claim: Under 164.502(g)(5), a covered entity may decline to treat a person as personal representative if it reasonably believes the individual has been or may be abused, neglected or endangered by that person, and judges that recognising them is not in the individual's best interest. The reproductive-health-care clause added by the 2024 rule was vacated nationwide in Purl v. HHS (N.D. Tex., June 18, 2025). The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal on Sept. 10, 2025.

Adult children: HHS guidance to parents says that once a son or daughter is an adult, the parent generally needs guardianship or a medical power of attorney to be their personal representative. Being the policyholder who covers the child as a dependent confers no HIPAA authority.
facts.source: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-individuals/mental-health/index.html ; HHS parent guidance PDF https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/when-your-child.pdf (fetch blocked; summarised from search results)

facts.claim: ACA rule 45 CFR 147.120: a plan that offers dependent coverage must offer it until the child turns 26 and may not condition it on financial dependency, residency, student status and similar factors. A plan may limit coverage to IRC 152(f)(1) children and may impose extra conditions on others, such as grandchildren. A second-degree relative (grandchild) is therefore often not a plan dependent unless adopted, fostered or under guardianship.

HIPAA's definition of 'family member' (45 CFR 160.103) covers dependents plus first- through fourth-degree relatives. Second-degree relatives are 'grandparents, grandchildren, aunts, uncles, nephews, and nieces'. Half-siblings count the same as full siblings, and in-laws and adoptive relatives the same as blood relatives. This definition supports the Rule's genetic-information (GINA) provisions. The pickup permission in 164.510(b) does not use it and turns on the patient identifying the person, not on kinship degree.

In a Dear Colleague letter dated Dec 3, 2025, OCR reminded regulated entities that parents who are personal representatives generally have a right to their minor children's records. It said denying that access can violate the Privacy Rule and named parental access an enforcement priority.

Minors and contraception (Guttmacher, 2026): 23 states plus DC explicitly let minors consent. 16 states allow it in specific circumstances (AZ, DE, FL, HI, IL, IN, KS, LA, MS, MO, MT, NJ, ND, OK, RI, TN). Idaho and Texas prohibit it without parental consent, and Texas applies that even at Title X clinics.

Minors and STIs (Guttmacher, as of July 2026): all 50 states and DC let minors consent to STI testing and treatment. 8 restrict this by age, and 16 have provisions that allow or require providers to notify parents in some cases.
45 CFR 164.522(b): providers must accommodate reasonable requests for confidential communications. Health plans must do so if the individual clearly states that disclosure could endanger them.

Guttmacher's dependent-confidentiality tracker lists six states that explicitly require insurers to give confidential communications when an insured dependent submits a written request: California, Colorado, Maryland, Massachusetts, Oregon and Washington. Some states have EOB-specific rules (e.g. New York, Wisconsin), and some protections apply only to adults or only to sensitive services.

No federal rule requires ID at a routine controlled-substance pickup. A 2013 CDC survey found 25 states with statutes that require or allow pharmacists to ask for ID (CT, DE, FL, GA, HI, ID, IL, IN, LA, ME, MA, MI, MN, NV, NM, NY, NC, ND, OK, OR, SC, TX, VT, VA, WV). Counting regulations as well, NAMSDL found 35 states in 2016, adding NJ, TN, UT, WI and WY. In most states ID is mandatory only when the pharmacist does not know the person (15 states in the CDC count).

Delaware (24 Del. Admin. Code CSA 4.0) is the universal case: staff must verify 'the identification of the receiver of the controlled substance prescription by reference to valid photographic identification' for every controlled substance. Accepted ID is a driver's license, Delaware ID or US passport, with federal and military ID added in 2016.

North Carolina G.S. 90-106.1 covers Schedule II and the combination Schedule III drugs. The person seeking the dispensation must show one of four unexpired government photo IDs (driver's license, NC special ID, military ID or passport) and need not be the patient. The pharmacy records that person's name, ID type and ID number and keeps them 3 years. Submitting them to the CSRS (the NC PDMP) satisfies the requirement to produce them.

NC Board of Pharmacy FAQ on S.L. 2011-349: a friend or family member may present their own ID and receive the prescription, and that person's ID must be documented. Board staff recommend that pharmacists 'ask patients to designate authorized pick up persons and document that authorization in the patient profile'.

Other ID-at-pickup rules:
- West Virginia: a valid government-issued photo ID before release of Schedule II–IV (2012).
- Georgia: demand, inspect and document ID for Schedule II pickups.
- New Mexico: verify ID for new Schedule II–IV prescriptions.
- Maine: ID only for out-of-state Schedule II prescriptions.
- Illinois: only a pharmacy ID policy is required, plus two IDs for Schedule V.
- New Jersey and Wisconsin: ID only when the person picking up is not the patient.
- Tennessee: government ID for opioids, benzodiazepines and some others above a 7-day supply.
- Nebraska: photo ID for opioids (2018).
- Washington: the prescriber notes on pain-management prescriptions that photo ID is required.

Idaho, Nevada and Minnesota relax their ID rules when insurance pays at least part of the claim. Idaho presumes identification when dispensing directly to the patient, and Nevada does not require ID when an insurer pays.

Massachusetts (105 CMR 700.012): a 'customer identifier' must be presented whenever a Schedule II–V controlled substance is dispensed, and the customer identification number is sent to the PMP (ASAP AIR05). The hardship exception requires the ultimate user or agent to print their name and address and sign. Naloxone is exempt (AIR04=99, AIR05='Naloxone').

Indiana's dispenser guide (ASAP 4.2A, Bamboo Health, 2024) says AIR05, the ID number of the person dropping off or picking up, is 'Required for Indiana retail pharmacies under IC 25-26-24-17(B)'. AIR06 (relationship) is only situational.

Wisconsin requires dispensers to collect the name of the person to whom a Schedule II or III drug is physically handed (2013 Act 199). Since April 9, 2017 the name is reported to the PDMP in AIR07/AIR08; for mail delivery the patient's name goes there. Wisconsin does not require AIR04–AIR06 (ID type, ID number, relationship). Source: WI ePDMP Data Submitter Guide, June 2026.

ASAP PDMP AIR segment, ASAP 4.2A/4.2B:
- AIR03: ID issuing jurisdiction.
- AIR04: ID qualifier (01 military, 02 state ID, 04 green card, 05 passport, 06 driver's license, 07 SSN, 08 tribal ID).
- AIR05: ID number of the person dropping off or picking up.
- AIR06: relationship of that person (01 Patient, 02 Parent/Legal Guardian, 03 Spouse, 04 Caregiver, 99 Other).
- AIR07/AIR08: that person's last and first name.
- AIR11: drop-off or pick-up qualifier.
ASAP 5.0 splits relationship into AIR06 (person picking up) and AIR23 (person dropping off), coded 01 Parent/Legal Guardian, 02 Spouse, 03 Caregiver, 99 Other. Neither version has a code for grandparent or other second-degree kin.

AIR06 (relationship) is marked situational, optional or not required in every state guide checked: Indiana, Missouri, Texas, Wisconsin, Nebraska and New York. No state found requires reporting the picker's relationship to the PDMP.
Utah requires the PDMP record to note the 'positive identification of the individual receiving the prescription, including the type of identification'.

Federal Controlled Substances Act, 21 U.S.C. 802(27): an 'ultimate user' is a person who has lawfully obtained and possesses a controlled substance 'for his own use or for the use of a member of his household or for an animal owned by him or by a member of his household'. No federal DEA rule specifies ID or authorization for an agent picking up at retail. CMS calls ID 'good practice' when the patient is unknown to pharmacy staff.

California Family Code 6550 (Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit): a relative caregiver such as a grandparent, aunt or uncle who completes items 1–8 gets the same medical and dental consent authority a guardian has under Probate Code 2353. Other states: Delaware's notarized caregiver affidavit lasts up to 1 year; Missouri's must be notarized and expires 1 year after delivery; Florida lets a relative consent when the parent cannot be reached, with no writing required. A grandparent without such paper 'has no more authority … than a stranger' (Oregon kinship guide).

NCPDP's D.0 payer-sheet template: Person Code is required 'if needed to uniquely identify the family members within the Cardholder ID'. In the Express Scripts commercial sheet, person codes run 001–010.

NCPDP SCRIPT NewRx carries a Patient (HumanPatient: identification, name, gender, date of birth, address, phone numbers) and a BenefitsCoordination block (payer, cardholder ID, cardholder name, group, PBM member ID). A dependent's e-prescription can therefore name the subscriber. No guardian, representative or relationship element appears in public schema models of 2017071. SCRIPT 2023011 becomes mandatory by Jan 1, 2028.

CMS-1696 (OMB 0938-0950, expires 12/31/2028) appoints a representative 'for your claim, appeal, grievance or request', with authority to make requests, present evidence, get information and receive communications. Section 2 asks for the representative's 'professional status or relationship to the person … (attorney, relative, etc.)'. The appointment is valid for one year from both signatures (42 CFR 405.910), and Part D forms go to the plan. It has nothing to do with dispensing or pickup.

Pharmacy family accounts:
- CVS: a parent can link a minor's prescription records (under 18) without the child's approval; an adult family member must authorise access.
- Walmart: adult dependents (18+) must approve before another adult manages their prescriptions; minors appear automatically.
- CVS Caremark Family Access: consenting adult family members let a designated manager view order histories, order refills and request new prescriptions.

Some PBMs and health systems cut parental visibility below 18:
- Optum Rx: dependents aged 13 and over must give permission before a parent sees their pharmacy information, and it 'does not list the specific medications prescribed to minors'.
- Kaiser Permanente Washington: proxy access for ages 13–17 is limited under Washington privacy law.
- Mass General Brigham: sensitive medications are hidden from both teen and parent portals.

Code-based pickup exists:
- Dartmouth Health lockers: the person collecting needs the patient's name, date of birth and a QR or unique pickup code.
- Southcentral Foundation: the patient gets a texted code that expires after two days, and the representative gives the code plus the patient's DOB. Controlled substances are barred from lockers by state regulation.
- Navy ScriptCenter: account holders pick pickup designees in settings.
- South Dakota remote pickup: identity must be verified, with photo ID if the person is not known.

Utah's ISO 18013-5 mobile driver's license pilot included a community health center pharmacy that accepts mDLs for transactions. The standard supports selective disclosure and offline verification of the issuer's signature. Whether boards of pharmacy accept an mDL for controlled-substance ID laws was not found.

implications: 1. HIPAA does not ask how anyone is related. Under 164.510(b) the only question is whether the patient, or someone standing in the patient's shoes, identified this person, or whether the pharmacist reasonably infers the patient wants it. Section 164.514(h) does not require formal verification for these disclosures. The circuit therefore needs a single predicate: 'this pickup is authorised for prescription R by the patient's own key, or by a credential that makes the holder the patient's personal representative'. Kinship degree, the family graph and the relationship code can all stay on phones.

2. 'Second degree' in the authority sense (patient <- guardian/parent <- delegate, e.g. a grandparent) matches the law exactly. The personal representative 'is treated as the individual' (164.502(g)(1)) and may in turn name 'any other person' (164.510(b)). The circuit can prove a chain of at most two signed delegations that is rooted at the patient's wallet, scoped PICKUP, bound to the prescription or drug class, unexpired and unrevoked (Merkle non-membership in a revocation set). A nullifier makes each authorisation single-use. The pharmacy learns only that the proof is valid. It does not learn whether there was one hop or two, who the middle link is, or the relationship. A grandparent who holds their own medical-consent authority (California caregiver affidavit, court guardianship) is a one-hop personal representative and needs no parent link.

3. 'Second degree' in the kinship sense (grandparent, aunt, uncle and so on) matters legally in only three places: (a) who can be a personal representative (parent, guardian, in loco parentis, a caregiver-affidavit relative under state law); (b) plan eligibility, since grandchildren are often excluded unless adopted, fostered or under guardianship (147.120); (c) HIPAA's GINA-only 'family member' definition. I recommend against building zero-knowledge 'kinship degree ≤ 2' proofs. They are legally unnecessary for pickup, and they would create a sensitive family-graph dataset. Prove authority, not kinship.

4. 'The prescriber indicates a dependent' should mean the prescription names the dependent's own wallet, never the parent's, so per-person accumulators and clinical checks stay one identity per person. The prescriber should also mark a 'minor-controlled / confidential' flag when the minor consented alone, a court or other person consented, or the parent agreed to confidentiality (164.502(g)(3)(i)(A)–(C)). For flagged prescriptions the circuit must refuse delegations rooted in a parent's personal-representative credential and accept only chains rooted in the minor's own key. The minor therefore needs a key of their own: a separate device or a minor-held secret. A parent-controlled dependent wallet is not enough.

5. Adults aged 18–26 on a parent's plan: the parent has no personal-representative status. Parent pickup works only if the adult child delegates from their own key. Turning 18 must automatically revoke parent-rooted credentials. State thresholds for confidential minor services vary (12, 13, 14, and by service), so age and service rules need to be per-state policy parameters, not constants.

6. Controlled substances: in several states the pharmacy, and sometimes the PDMP, must see and record the identity of the person picking up:
- Delaware: all controlled substances.
- North Carolina: Schedule II and combination Schedule III; name, ID type and number, kept 3 years and reportable to the CSRS.
- West Virginia: Schedule II–IV.
- Georgia: Schedule II.
- New Mexico: new Schedule II–IV prescriptions.
- Massachusetts: Schedule II–V; ID number sent in AIR05.
- Indiana: ID number sent in AIR05.
- Wisconsin: name sent in AIR07/08 for Schedule II–III.
- Utah: ID type recorded.
- Tennessee and Nebraska: some opioids and other drugs.
The design cannot hide who the picker is from the pharmacy in those cases, but it can hide the relationship and the intermediary. AIR06 is optional in every guide checked, and the zero-knowledge proof makes it unnecessary. The physical ID check binds the human; the proof supplies the authority. Where a board accepts mDLs, an ISO 18013-5 selective-disclosure check could reveal only the name and ID number the law requires.

7. A larger conflict for controlled substances: every state PDMP collects the patient's own name, date of birth and address in the ASAP PAT segment from the dispensing pharmacy. Rule I2 (only wallet ID and proofs leave the phone) therefore cannot hold for controlled-substance dispensing. A lawful design needs a disclosure path from phone to pharmacy to PDMP that is narrow, logged and consented to for controlled substances. That is a separate decision from pickup, but the picker's ID fields travel in the same record.

8. North Carolina's Board recommends that patients 'designate authorized pick up persons' and that the pharmacy document this in the patient profile. A delegation commitment recorded on the sequencer, with the pharmacy storing the verified proof and its nullifier as the dispensing record, can serve as that documentation without the pharmacy keeping relationship data. This strengthens the design's legal defensibility compared with today's bare prescriptionId at POST /dispensing/dispense.

9. Ordinary NCPDP claims already tell the pharmacy and the payer the policyholder's name (312-CC/313-CD), the relationship (306-C6), the person code (303-C3) and dependent status (309-C9). zpk's per-person wallets plus an opaque bound family hash are already more private than the industry standard. Keep it that way: the family hash and the insurer's approval must never encode role (parent, child, spouse, student, disabled dependent). Accumulator pooling needs only 'W is in family F under plan P'.

10. Confidential communications law reaches into the app:
- California AB 1184 / Civil Code 56.107: sensitive-service communications go to the protected individual, not the policyholder.
- Six states (CA, CO, MD, MA, OR, WA) require confidential communications on a dependent's request.
- 164.522(b): plans must accommodate requests where the individual says disclosure could endanger them.
In zpk the policyholder's phone must not itemise a dependent's prescriptions in family accumulator or deductible views, pickup lists or messaging. It may show pooled totals only. Extra family NFC cards mailed to the insured member must not grant read access to other members' claims.

11. The 2025 OCR letter cuts the other way: over-hiding from parents of minors is also an enforcement risk. Parent-rooted access should be the default for minors, except where a minor-consent exception or a state law applies, and should not be blocked wholesale.

12. CMS-1696 covers Medicare claims, appeals, grievances and requests, is valid one year, and has nothing to do with pickup. The repo's AOR flow (aor-data.ts, aor-service.ts) uses it as a pickup authority with a 48-hour cool-down that no law requires. Reuse the commitment and revocation machinery, but root pickup authority in:
- (a) the patient's own designation (164.510(b));
- (b) personal-representative credentials: guardianship order, health care POA, caregiver affidavit or parent of an unemancipated minor.
The form itself names the relationship ('relative, attorney'), so it rightly stays on the phone. Revocation must take effect immediately, both for abuse cases under 164.502(g)(5) and when a minor turns 18.

13. Personal-representative status, unlike a 164.510 designee, must be verified (164.514(h)). Someone must check the paper once: the insurer or enrollment authority, a notary-style attester, or the pharmacist at first use. That party then issues a signed credential such as 'holder is personal representative of W, scope, expiry', with the relationship and document type left out. Afterwards the circuit proves possession of an unexpired, unrevoked credential. The repo's existing representative wallet type (domain tag 3, ProofGate.verifyRepresentative) is the natural home. The DelegationRegistry relationship codes (1 Parent … 6 Appointed Rep) should never leave the phone.

14. Existing practice supports a token or code model for non-controlled drugs: locker codes plus DOB with a 2-day expiry, app-designated pickup persons, and family accounts where adults must consent. A zero-knowledge pickup token is a privacy-preserving version of something pharmacies already accept. For controlled substances, lockers are typically barred by state rules and ID laws apply, so the proof supplements the ID check rather than replacing it.

15. Pharmacist judgment cannot be designed away. 164.510(b)(3) and 164.502(g)(5) leave the final call to the pharmacist. The pharmacy UI should show the result ('authorised by patient or representative: yes or no; controlled substance: ID required in this state') and let the pharmacist refuse. It must never show the relationship.

facts.claim: 'Second-degree relative' in medicine means one intervening relative in the bloodline: aunt, uncle, grandparent, grandchild, niece, nephew, half-sibling (about a quarter of genes shared). First-degree means parent, child, sibling.

facts.claim: The legal civil-law count gives a different answer. Siblings and grandparents are both 2nd degree, aunt/uncle is 3rd and first cousins are 4th. The common-law count differs for collateral kin (uncle and nephew are 2nd degree under common law, 3rd under civil law). So 'second degree' means different relatives in medicine and in law.

So the medical second-degree set is not 'every 2-hop path'. Proving kinship would also need a genealogy graph that no actor in this system attests (the plan family hash covers only subscriber and dependents).

facts.claim: HIPAA does not require proof of relationship for pickup. Under 45 CFR 164.510(b) a pharmacist may use professional judgment to let a friend or family member pick up a filled prescription, and a person who arrives and names a specific prescription is treated as involved in the patient's care. A patient's objection overrides this.

Some states require the identity, but not the relationship, of whoever picks up a controlled substance. Massachusetts requires a 'customer identifier' (the ID number from a government ID of the person picking up) for Schedule II-V drugs and reports it to the PMP (105 CMR 700.012(A), 247 CMR 9.04). Minnesota 152.11 requires photo ID from the purchaser of Schedule II/III drugs, who need not be the patient. North Dakota 61-04-03.1 requires positive ID when the picker's identity is uncertain.

The PMP reporting standard field AIR06 'Relationship of Person Dropping Off or Picking Up Rx' was situational in ASAP 4.2A and marked not used in ASAP 4.2B (effective 7/1/23). The picker's ID fields remain.

So a grandchild can be a plan dependent of a grandparent subscriber. That information sits with the employer/HR Tool, which under I5/I6 must not link it to wallets.

No federal law gives minors a right to confidential contraception or STI care, but many states let minors consent on their own (Guttmacher counted 21 states plus DC for all minors' contraceptive consent). facts.claim: Delegatable anonymous credentials (Belenkiy, Camenisch, Chase, Kohlweiss, Lysyanskaya, Shacham, CRYPTO 2009, 'Randomizable Proofs and Delegatable Anonymous Credentials', ePrint 2008/428) let a credential be re-delegated along a chain while hiding the delegators. The construction uses randomizable Groth-Sahai NIZK proofs, and proof size is O(L*k) in chain length L, against k^Omega(2^L) for the earlier Chase-Lysyanskaya 2006 scheme.

Later delegatable-credential work: Crites and Lysyanskaya, CT-RSA 2019 (mercurial signatures, ePrint 2018/923), which lets an adversarial issuer in the chain detect when the credential is shown. Griffy, Lysyanskaya, Mir, Perez Kempner and Slamanig, ASIACRYPT 2024 (ePrint 2024/1216), fixes that leak. Mir, Slamanig, Bauer and Mayrhofer, PoPETs 2023 (ePrint 2022/680), adds attributes, hidden delegator identities and limits on further delegation (SPSEQ-UC). All are pairing-based.

The pairing-based schemes (delegatable credentials, BBS on BLS12-381, CL/Idemix on RSA groups) cannot be verified natively by o1js 2.13. Its in-circuit curves are only Secp256k1, Secp256r1, Pallas and Vesta, and there is no pairing gadget. The o1js-native equivalent of a delegatable credential is a SNARK over Poseidon-committed delegation leaves in a Merkle tree, in the style of zk-creds and Semaphore.

zk-creds (Rosenberg, White, Garman, Miers, IEEE S&P 2023, ePrint 2022/878) removes the need for issuers to hold signing keys by issuing credentials to a bulletin board (a transparency log, a Byzantine system or a blockchain). It turns existing identity documents into anonymous credentials and composes statements across several credentials. The passport age-check showing takes under 150 ms.

Semaphore v4: a group is a Merkle tree of identity commitments. A proof shows membership without saying which member. The nullifier is the hash of a public scope and the identity's secret key, so each identity can make one valid proof per scope.

SD-JWT is RFC 9901 (Nov 2025). Hidden claims are salted digests under one issuer signature, and a Key Binding JWT proves possession of the holder key. ISO/IEC 18013-5 mdoc works the same way: salted digests in the signed MSO plus a device key. Both selectively disclose but are linkable across presentations, because the same signature, digests and device key are reused. That is why Google's Longfellow-zk (Frigo and shelat, ePrint 2024/2010) runs ZK over the ECDSA/SHA-256 mdoc; it is deployed in Google Wallet.

The W3C Data Integrity BBS Cryptosuites (working draft) use BBS signatures for selective disclosure with unlinkable derived proofs. The signature is pairing-based, so a verifier would have to check BBS outside o1js.

Macaroons (Birgisson et al., NDSS 2014) are bearer credentials built from chained HMACs. Any holder can add caveats that narrow when, where, by whom and for what a credential is accepted, then pass it on, with no central authority. This is a model for a guardian narrowing a grant to one prescription before passing it to a grandparent, though it is neither anonymous nor zero-knowledge.

mina-attestations (zkSecurity, built on o1js) is an existing o1js credential library. It has native credentials (Mina Schnorr signature), imported credentials (an external proof verified by recursion, with ECDSA and RSA imports) and owner binding to a Mina public key. Presentations are bound to a context hash of verifier, action, server nonce, client nonce, vk hash and claims, to stop replay. It claims unlinkability, but its README describes no revocation or nullifiers. Hacken's January 2025 audit lists 11 findings (4 resolved, 7 accepted).

The installed o1js is 2.13.0. Its top level exports Nullifier, MerkleMap, MerkleTree/MerkleWitness, IndexedMerkleMap, ZkProgram, SelfProof, DynamicProof (verify(vk) and verifyIf(vk, cond) check another program's proof against a supplied verification key), verify, Encryption, Crypto, Gadgets (including and/xor), Hash (SHA2_256) and the foreign-curve ECDSA. A method can verify at most 2 proofs (maxProofsVerified 0|1|2).

o1js Nullifier implements PLUME (Gupta and Gurkan, ePrint 2022/1255): a deterministic nullifier h(m,pk)^sk with h = Poseidon.hashToGroup(message || pk). verify(message) checks a Chaum-Pedersen-style equation in-circuit. The struct contains the publicKey, so to stay anonymous the Nullifier must be a private input and only key() = Poseidon(nullifier point) made public. The nullifier is created outside the circuit by mina-signer createNullifier(message, privateKey) with a Mina (Pallas) key. assertUnused/setUsed use a MerkleMapWitness.

Constraint rows measured on o1js 2.13 with Provable.constraintSystem / analyzeMethods: Poseidon.hash of 8 fields 52; MerkleWitness(32).calculateRoot 450; IndexedMerkleMap(32) assertIncluded 475, assertNotIncluded 531; Mina Signature.verify 349; Nullifier.verify 713; Field.lessThanOrEqual 39; ECDSA P-256 verifySignedHash 40,194; SHA-256 of 128 bytes 14,410. A flat two-hop pickup circuit sketch (2 delegation memberships, 2 revocation non-memberships, date window checks, a nullifier and a per-pharmacy pseudonym) came to 2,284 rows. A SelfProof step shows 513 rows, but analyzeMethods does not count the recursive verifier that Pickles adds.

facts.claim: Proving in this codebase takes 25-31 s per registration or credential proof, and 25-45 s per device proof on the workstation. Every recursive hop is another full proof of that kind. Proofs pinned to the ledger's exact current roots are invalidated by any transition that lands while proving (finding A-33).

A serialized o1js proof here (maxProofsVerified 0) is 22,382 bytes binary, 29,844 base64 characters. That is about 25x the 888-byte user memory of the NTAG216 the NFC attestation targets, and larger than the 8 KB maximum of DESFire EV3.

facts.claim: o1js 2.13 has no Ed25519/EdDSA gadget (zero hits in the dist). The sequencer's Ed25519-signed NFC attestations therefore cannot be checked inside a circuit. A Pallas Schnorr signature (349 rows) can.

o1js Encryption.encrypt works inside a circuit: it witnesses an ephemeral scalar, does ECDH by Group.scale and encrypts with a Poseidon sponge plus an authentication tag. A circuit can therefore output a ciphertext of a hidden attribute (such as the relationship code) under an auditor's public key and prove that it encrypts the value actually used. This is verifiable escrow.

IndexedMerkleMap: maximum height 52. The docs claim 4-8x fewer constraints than MerkleMap and mark it experimental. It can be used as a private input inside a ZkProgram (the provable part is root plus length; the tree data stays on the prover's side). assertNotIncluded gives non-membership, which suits revocation sets. The prover needs the map's contents, or a witness for its key, to prove non-inclusion.
o1js MerkleTree(h) holds 2^(h-1) leaves. DELEGATION_TREE_HEIGHT = 8, so the delegation registry holds 128 leaves: a very small anonymity set for hidden-leaf membership proofs.

The current delegation leaf is unsalted: DelegationData.commitment() = Poseidon(delegatorWalletId, delegateWalletId, scopeFlags, effectiveDate, expirationDate, relationshipCode, delegationHash). Anyone who knows the two wallet IDs can brute-force the relationship (6 codes, 8 scope values, a small date range).
The engine's DelegationRegistry keeps the plaintext DelegationData, relationship code included, in an in-memory map next to the leaf, so the engine sees every relationship.

PortableDelegationCredential, the existing offline pickup credential, carries in clear the delegator wallet, the delegate wallet, relationshipCode, the leaf index and the Merkle witness. A pharmacy verifying it learns the relationship. AOR sets a 48 h PICKUP cool-down and a 4 h offline TTL.

PrescriptionData binds the patient through memberWalletId and has no pickup-policy field. AccessControlProgram takes currentDate as a private input, so the prover chooses the date that its expiry check runs against.

The current NFC attestation is a bearer token. Its own design notes say nothing on the tag is secret, it is an Ed25519-signed receipt of wallet ID, credential commitment and forest root with a 24 h default expiry, and its nonce is a revocation handle, not an authentication factor. A copied tag replays.

NTAG 424 DNA has AES-128 with 5 customer keys, SUN (a CMAC-authenticated message per tap), 3-pass mutual authentication and optional LRP, and is Common Criteria EAL4. Everything is symmetric, so the verifier must hold the AES key or ask a backend that does. It cannot prove anything to an offline pharmacy that does not share the secret.

Secure-element cards (JavaCard; Java Card 3.0.5 adds AES-CMAC, ECDH, PACE; JCOP-class cards support ECDSA, with the curve depending on the chip) and FIDO2 NFC authenticators can hold a non-exportable asymmetric key and sign a challenge. FIDO2 defaults to ES256 (P-256) and uses a separate credential per relying party, so the same key does not appear at two relying parties. None of these devices can run an o1js prover.
