design.effort_estimate:
Core work (P1 to P3) is about 25 to 35 engineer-days, roughly 6 to 8 sessions at this program's pace.

- P1, about 10-14 days: phone-to-phone tickets, assuming dependents have their own phones. Covers the ticket library; PickupProgram.claim with tests; engine storage, routes, checkpointing and audit events; the finalize gate in dispensePrescription; the pharmacy challenge, present and verify routes plus the dashboard; automatic registration and holder mode on the member device; QR pairing; and the e2e harness steps.
- P2, about 8-12 days: custodial dependent wallets. Covers multi-wallet NautilusStateData, dependent enrollment on the guardian's phone, the co-parent transfer, CustodyProgram, handover at majority through WalletMigrationService, and custodial view filtering.
- P3, about 6-9 days: the no-phone and confidential paths. Covers the NTAG216 family pickup card and the Tier R reveal, printed slips, the prescriber's pickupLock with the minor's self key and slip, pooled-only family views, and removing the existing relationship leaks.

Smallest release-one slice, about 6-8 days: Tier R only, with dependents on their own phones. It needs no new circuit; it has per-prescription one-time secrets, the engine ticket set, and the server-side pickup gate.

Optional P4, about 6-10 days: the transfer circuit, the pairing mailbox, pseudonyms, and JavaCard or FIDO2 cards.

Controlled substances are deferred with release one. When they come into scope, the pharmacy side (state rule table, local ID log, PDMP export) is about 4-6 days, apart from the separate PAT-segment disclosure decision.

The estimate assumes B3's adjudicate-then-finalize lands first or alongside, and that proving time on handsets is acceptable. It has not been measured yet.
risks: Controller unavailable. Every prescription needs the controller's phone to register a set once. A hospitalised or incapacitated adult, a lost phone or a dead battery blocks new tickets. Mitigations: the recovery card restores the wallet; a co-controller key for a verified POA or guardian; the counter fallback. The co-controller key is a standing grant under another name, which is the honest weak point compared with standing delegations.

Custodial key equals full control. A parent holding W_C's enrollment key can sign as W_C and decrypt every message to W_C. Abuse and custody changes need an insurer-verified migration (164.502(g)(5)), which is heavy. Coverage is not the same as authority: a policyholder who is a non-custodial parent may have no right to make medical decisions under a custody order, and dependent enrollment from the HR roster (family_id only) cannot detect that.

Confidential leak through accumulators. The B3 accumulator change lands on the credential the custodial phone holds. It needs withholding or monthly pooling for locked prescriptions; contraception is usually zero cost share, so it moves nothing.

Bearer tiers. A Tier R card or slip is a bearer token until used. Theft plus the PIN, or a slip with no PIN, allows pickup of the prescriptions loaded on it. The damage is limited to those prescriptions and their short expiry, and Tier R is refused for CONTROLLED. A passive NTAG216 card cannot answer a challenge.

Proving latency and size. Pickles' fixed cost (25-45 s on the desktop here) dominates even a circuit under 150 rows, handsets are unmeasured, and a proof is about 22 KB, which no QR code holds. Mitigations: pre-proving with a session key, upload or NFC/BLE transport, and Tier R as the fallback at the counter.

Pharmacist judgment and the human channel. The pharmacist sees the picker, and an older adult collecting a child's prescription suggests a grandparent. The design hides the relationship and the intermediary from records and the network, not from what the pharmacist sees. Opting into the per-pharmacy pseudonym links the same holder across different patients at that pharmacy, so it is off by default.

Metadata. In P1, delivery to holders goes through the OS share sheet or messaging apps, outside zpk's guarantees. A P4 mailbox and online presentation uploads expose IP addresses. A set re-registered right after a visit reveals a revocation's timing.

Trust in the engine. Lock, expiry, custody and set membership are enforced by the engine, which today runs inside the sequencer and can act as any member (A-2, B1/B2). Pickup privacy does not depend on the engine, but whether it is enforced does.

Prescriber attestation for confidential prescriptions. Letting a prescriber attest that a minor consented alone, in place of B5's device consent, is a consent bypass that could be abused. Limit it to custodial wallets, single prescriptions and services on the state table, and audit it.

B3 coupling. Finalizing by ticket and having the controller's device apply the accumulator change later changes B3's interface. B3's open questions (the read-then-write reservation window, mail order with no counter moment) carry over.

Legal open items: whether a bare ticket meets the documentation North Carolina's board recommends; mDL acceptance under state ID laws; the patient's identity in the PDMP PAT segment against I2; agents outside the household and 'ultimate user'; how insurer-paid relaxations (ID, NV, MN) apply; and the per-state law on confidential services for minors, which changes every year.

Load and abuse. Automatic registration roughly doubles engine writes per prescription. /pickup/present takes uploads from parties that are not enrolled, so it needs rate limits and must verify the proof before storing it.

findings.attack: Device and transport co-location. Custodial wallets run on the parent's single member node. Today the wallet is registered by a node-signed l2_registerEntity (src/nodes/routes/member-routes.ts:687). The sequencer logs every node-signed call as '[admin] <method> by <nodeId>' (src/l2/l2-rpc-server.ts:807). The device keeps a node-signed /events SSE subscription open (src/security/node-roles.ts member: GET:/events; src/l2/l2-client.ts:559). Wallet-signed calls leave from the same IP and process (src/nodes/nautilus-app-server.ts:336). Registering W_C, fetching W_C's eScripts and ready notices, requesting W_C attestations and registering W_C's ticket sets from that phone all tie W_C to W_P. The co-parent's phone ties W_C to W_S. Bursts tie a household together: one sync processes eScripts for W_P, W_C1 and W_C2; a 'revoke Grandma' or lost-card action re-registers sets for several children at the same instant.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: The engine, the sequencer and replica logs learn which adult wallet controls which minor wallet, the first-degree parent-to-child edge, and the sibling sets. Together with custodialUntil (a 'minor' bit) and the B8 family binding, the roles can be inferred. This contradicts two claims in the design: that it hides which custodian signed, and that the sequencer learns no family link. The grandparent holder is not exposed by this.
findings.mitigation: Give each wallet its own network identity. A custodial wallet must never register or stream through the parent's node key: use a wallet-signed registration, not a node-signed one. Send wallet-signed traffic through an unlinkable relay that the sequencer does not operate (OHTTP-style), or at least over separate connections with per-wallet randomized schedules. Jitter and batch set registrations and revocations. State honestly that the engine already knows co-family membership through B8.

findings.attack: Custody is self-attested, so a policyholder can capture an adult dependent. The GroupEnrollmentToken carries no identity binding: only tokenId, group, plan, employeeId, familyId, validUntil, issuer and nonce (src/onboarding/group-enrollment-token.ts:113-125). The date of birth in the wallet preimage is typed on whichever phone redeems the code (src/wallets/wallet-derivation.ts:115-131). Codes reach the employee, and each token can be consumed only once (src/onboarding/token-authority.ts:223). A policyholder redeems a 22-year-old's code, or a spouse's, on their own phone and enters a false date of birth. CustodyProgram then proves 'minor' without complaint, because it proves consistency with the preimage, not with reality.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: The adult dependent is locked out of their own wallet. The policyholder decrypts every eScript sent to that wallet (the X25519 key derives from the enrollment key), signs B5 consent, registers tickets and sees the accumulators. This breaks the AB 1184-style confidential-communication rules and the 18-26 analysis in the design, and it enables coercive control of a spouse.
findings.mitigation: The employer already holds the date of birth, so having it sign a coarse custody field into each dependent's token discloses nothing new: for example 'custodial-eligible until CCYY-MM', or a Pallas-signed date-of-birth commitment that CustodyProgram must open. Tokens for adults refuse custodial redemption. Deliver adult dependents' codes to the dependent's own contact, not to the employee. Add an insurer-assisted reclaim path that voids a captured wallet.

findings.attack: The parent controls the handover at majority, and co-parents share one key. W_C's enrollment key and recovery card are created on the parent's phone. WalletMigrationService accepts whoever holds the old key or the recovery card (src/wallets/wallet-migration-service.ts:107-150). When custody lapses, the engine cannot tell the young adult's W_C-key signature from the parent's, because the key is the same. A controlling parent can migrate W_C to a key only they hold. In a custody dispute, whichever co-parent migrates first locks the other out. There is no per-custodian key the engine could revoke under 164.502(g)(5). The parent can also decrypt every message stored for W_C before migration, since there is no forward secrecy.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: The young adult may never gain control, so the age-out revocation in the design does not work. An abusive custodian keeps full access to the wallet, and the other parent can be hijacked out of it.
findings.mitigation: Register individually revocable custodian sub-keys under W_C instead of copying the shared enrollment key between phones. Handover should require something the parent lacks: a fresh age-out token issued by the employer or insurer to the dependent's own contact, plus a notice-and-wait period visible to every custodian. Rotate the encryption keys at handover and expire old ciphertexts.

findings.attack: The Tier R card reuses the card cryptography the codebase retired. The design proposes scrypt plus AES-GCM under a PIN, the v2 format (src/security/recovery-card.ts:114-215, SCRYPT_N = 2^15). The NTAG216 is readable by any phone, and the GCM tag lets an attacker test PINs offline. The v3 notes in the same file (recovery-card.ts:240-249, PRD-1) say exactly this: 'a card must yield nothing to unlimited offline compute'. A 4-6 digit PIN falls in minutes to hours, and 'three wrong PINs' only applies at the counter. Separately, the PIN is typed on the pharmacy keypad, so the pharmacy can decrypt all five tickets on the card, including other grandchildren's and other pharmacies' prescriptions. The static cardId and the clear rxRef (8 bytes of rxBinding) give the pharmacy a pseudonym the holder never opted into, across visits and patients, and let anyone holding audit-chain rxBindings tie a skimmed card to W_C's prescription.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: A stolen or found card is a bearer pickup token. The pharmacy can link siblings and track a repeat picker. Pickups of other tickets on the card can be forged once their secrets are known.
findings.mitigation: Use the v3 split pattern. The card carries only a random handle and a one-time-pad share. The engine holds the other share for each ticket and releases it against an attempt-limited PIN verifier, only for the rxBinding and pharmacyWalletId being dispensed. Put no rxRef on the card: the terminal asks the engine which handles match prescriptions it holds. Make cardId per-load or per-ticket. Make every Tier R ticket single-fill.

findings.attack: The confidential-minor path leaks through state keyed to W_C. The custodial phone must prove W_C's credential updates (the B1 step-two queue). Each WalletUpdatePayload carries a reason ('fill', 'prior-auth', 'reversal') and a timestamp (src/credentials/wallet-update.ts:52-68), and the accumulator leaf changes on every fill (src/adjudication/interactive-service.ts:3391). A withheld or monthly batch still shows that something happened and how much, and the pooled family accumulator moves. Every other path keyed to W_C must also be filtered: PA decisions, step therapy, reversals, D4 refusals, refill notices, the PCP and authorization lists. One miss discloses. A parent who taps W_C's attestation at /nfc/scan receives that wallet's full drug history (src/nodes/routes/pharmacy-routes.ts:918-1049). A slip whose PIN is optional is a bearer token if the parent finds it. Separately, the minor cannot prove ownership of W_C at a confidential visit, because only the custodial phone can obtain W_C's attestation. A sibling can therefore present the other child's W_C.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: The parent learns that confidential (sensitive-service) fills exist and how much they cost, and possibly the drug through history routes. This is exactly what 164.502(g)(3) and state minor-consent law protect. Wrong-patient prescriptions are also possible.
findings.mitigation: Keep confidential prescriptions off W_C's custodial credential. Issue them to a minor-held sub-identity whose accumulator joins the family pool only as insurer-side pooled entries, or hold their accumulator effects at the engine. /nfc/scan and every route serving W_C must exclude locked prescriptions for every caller. Add a test that a custodial-signed caller sees no trace of a locked prescription. Bind the minor's self-key to W_C at a prior event that is not locked.

findings.attack: The prescriber's minor-consent attestation and prescriber-printed slips form a consent bypass and a diversion channel hidden from parents. A pediatric prescriber knows many custodial wallet IDs. It writes locked prescriptions for high-value drugs that are not controlled (GLP-1s, for example), using its own key as 'the minor's self key' or printing the slips itself. An accomplice collects them through Tier R. The custodial view filters locked prescriptions, so no parent ever sees them, and the plan pays.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Fraud on children's coverage that the people best placed to notice it cannot see. B5 consent is bypassed.
findings.mitigation: A lock key must be a minor key already registered under W_C, or come with a minor ProofGate proof. Restrict locks to the service and drug classes in the state table. Have the insurer analyse locked-prescription rates per prescriber. Require a PIN the minor chooses on slips. Apply quantity caps.

findings.attack: A revoked or expired slot is honoured if the bag leaves before the engine finalizes. /interactive/fill runs as an asynchronous proving job (src/nodes/routes/pharmacy-routes.ts:454-616, dispensingJobs) that takes 25-45 s or more per proof behind the D7 proving lease. Pharmacists will hand the bag over on the local check against a cache up to 4 h old. The design says the pharmacy 'keeps the bag', which assumes they wait.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: A lost card or an abusive ex whose slot was just revoked still collects. The refusal at finalize only withholds the pharmacy's payment.
findings.mitigation: Add a cheap synchronous engine check before handover (set version current, slot unrevoked, not spent), separate from the slow proving finalize. Push revocations to subscribed pharmacies. Allow offline acceptance only for drugs that are not controlled, with the pharmacy carrying the liability.

findings.attack: Policy bits are not enforced. PickupProgram.claim takes policy as a private input and asserts only the ticket opening, so the engine never sees singleFill. Because spentKey = Poseidon(D_SPENT, T, fillNo) is per fill, the same T can be spent again at fill 2 and fill 3. For Tier R, the revealed s, seen by the terminal, the pharmacy and any logs, is reusable at the next refill unless single-fill is forced. transferDepth = 0 cannot stop a holder from sharing hs or the session key. The PickupProgram.transfer slot rotation also tells the engine that a second hop exists.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: A single-use grant becomes reusable. A pharmacy can forge evidence for later refills of a Tier R ticket. The hop count, which the design says is hidden, is revealed whenever a transfer happens.
findings.mitigation: Expose singleFill as a public output, or output a per-ticket nullifier, and spend per ticket when the bit is set. Force single-fill for all Tier R tickets. Drop the transfer circuit, or have controllers emit cover rotations, and document that tickets are transferable.

findings.attack: The engine or the operator can inject tickets. The pharmacy checks T against the set served by GET /interactive/pickup-tickets and never verifies W_C's signature over that set. The engine runs inside the sequencer (A-2), and the operator may rewrite any entity's signing key (src/l2/l2-rpc-server.ts:2013-2017). An insider adds a T whose opening it knows and collects any patient's prescription; a Tier R ticket needs no proof at all.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Drug diversion and false finalization. The integrity of pickup rests entirely on the engine.
findings.mitigation: The pharmacy verifies the controller's Ed25519 signature over (rxBinding, T0..T3, setExpiry, version) against the key registry. The audit event carries the hash of the signed set. Alert on any signing-key change for a wallet.

findings.attack: 'Automatic' registration needs an unlocked key, and the controller is unavailable in exactly the typical second-degree case. walletSigner returns null while device state is locked (src/nodes/nautilus-app-server.ts:320-330; src/nodes/nautilus-local-state.ts:236, 432, 452). Background registration therefore means either keeping W_C's enrollment key decrypted in memory, which weakens I3, or the parent unlocking the phone for every eScript. When the parent is hospitalised and the grandparent collects, no ticket set exists and the counter fallback does not apply. The only remedy left is the co-controller key, which is a standing grant under another name.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Availability fails in the scenario that motivates the question. Pressure to keep keys unlocked weakens I3.
findings.mitigation: Register a narrowly scoped ticket-issuing subkey under W_C, held in the OS keystore and usable without the PIN. It can register ticket sets for W_C's prescriptions and do nothing else (no decryption, no consent). Alternatively, let the controller pre-sign a few blank short-lived ticket sets that bind to a prescription on first use.

findings.attack: Two custodial phones race. Both parents' phones receive W_C's eScript and each registers a set automatically. The second registration replaces the first, dropping the first parent's holders. The engine sees two registrations from two devices seconds apart.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Some holders fail at the counter without warning. The engine learns that the household has two custodians and which device is which.
findings.mitigation: Designate one issuing device per dependent; the others ask it phone-to-phone. Or define a deterministic merge with a fixed slot budget that the engine cannot attribute to a device.

findings.attack: Controlled substances: legally required records reveal the relationship. In states with ID laws, the pharmacy records the picker's driving licence (name, date of birth, address). The PDMP receives both the AIR picker fields and the patient's PAT name, date of birth and address. A shared surname and address with a 50-year age gap says 'grandparent' without AIR06. New Jersey and Wisconsin require ID only when the picker is not the patient, so the pharmacist must learn whether the picker is the patient, which the protocol hides. Under I1/I2 the pharmacy does not even know who the patient is.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: For controlled substances the relationship can be inferred by the pharmacy and the PDMP. The claim that the relationship stays hidden even here does not hold.
findings.mitigation: Keep controlled substances out of release one, as planned. When they are added: in the NJ and WI cases, ask for ID from everyone rather than reveal whether the picker is the patient; say plainly that the relationship can be inferred in these states; and settle the PAT disclosure decision first.

findings.attack: The insurer as paperwork verifier. POA and guardian co-controller keys, emancipation, and abuse or custody migrations are all 'insurer-verified'. The insurer reads the court order or POA, which carries names and the relationship, and binds the outcome to W. GET /interactive/family-history still shows family composition (B8).
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: The relationship and identity data reach the insurer linked to the wallet, which breaks I1/I2 and the design's claim that no relationship is stored anywhere.
findings.mitigation: Use blind attestation. The verifier signs a Pallas credential over a salted commitment to the principal's identity, not over W, and the phone proves in ZK that W's preimage matches. The engine records only that a co-controller key was added. Remove relationship labels from family-history, as the design already proposes.

findings.attack: Phone proving and transport. The claim circuit is about 150 rows, but Pickles' fixed step-and-wrap overhead dominates, and it has never been measured on a phone. The 25-45 s figures are desktop numbers for larger circuits. o1js needs WASM threads (SharedArrayBuffer with cross-origin isolation), roughly 1-2 GB peak memory, and compiled or cached prover keys on the device. A 22 KB proof does not fit in a QR code, and iOS restricts NFC card emulation, leaving upload or BLE. Grandparents often have older phones.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Tier Z may be unusable on the holder's phone, which pushes users onto the weaker Tier R.
findings.mitigation: Replace Tier Z with one-time prekeys. At pairing the holder gives the controller a batch of one-time Ed25519 public keys, topped up later through the mailbox. Each ticket is T = Poseidon(D_TICKET, rxBinding, H(pk_i), policy, salt). At the counter the holder reveals pk_i, salt and policy and signs the challenge with sk_i. This keeps the same unlinkability (each key is used once) and keystore holder binding, with no circuit, no proving, and about 100 bytes that fit in a QR code or NFC exchange. The claim proof binds to no ledger root, so the A-33/D8 lease never applies to it; only the dispense finalize still runs under the lease.

findings.attack: rxBinding can be found by dictionary attack from the audit chain. rxBinding = Poseidon(D, PrescriptionData.commitment(), hashString(rxId), lockKeyHash). rxId is `RX-${Date.now()}-${4 base36 chars}` (src/nodes/routes/prescriber-routes.ts:450, 551). The sequencer stores threadIdHash = hashString(`rx-${rxId}`) beside the eScript metadata (prescriber, W_C, timestamp), so about 10^9-10^10 guesses recover rxId. PrescriptionData is unsalted, so the formulary, quantity, refills and dates complete the search.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Replica operators and audit readers recover the drug. A failed match with lockKeyHash = 0 tells them the prescription is confidential, i.e. a sensitive service.
findings.mitigation: Add a random 128-bit rxSalt, carried inside the encrypted eScript, to rxBinding, and make rxId 128-bit random.

findings.attack: Revocation and re-registration patterns. Replacing only the revoked slot shows the engine which slot changed, and the spent records carry slot indexes, so the engine can see that 'the holder who collected fills 1-3 was just revoked'. A lost-card or holder revocation re-registers sets across several siblings at once. Tier Z versus Tier R hints whether the picker has a phone.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Weak behavioural signals plus sibling linkage.
findings.mitigation: Re-salt every slot on any re-registration and redeliver the openings. Add cover re-registrations with jitter. Do not record the slot index or tier at the engine.

findings.attack: Holder device theft and NFC relay. The session key is generated ahead of time and the app answers challenges. A stolen unlocked phone, or a relay rig near the holder, can collect at the counter.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Bearer pickup of the tickets on that phone.
findings.mitigation: Gate session-key signing on user presence (biometric). Show the pharmacy name before signing. Give presentations a short TTL.

findings.attack: Other low-severity issues. CustodyProgram makes majorityYears public, which reveals the state class (19 for AL and NE, 21 for MS). The year of lapse narrows the birth date, and the custodial bit is itself a 'minor' label. /pickup/present accepts uploads from unauthenticated parties, so it can be flooded to burn proof-verification CPU. North Carolina's board recommends documenting 'designated pickup persons' in the patient profile, which may be read as requiring names.
findings.what_breaks_or_leaks: Minor metadata, denial of service, and legal uncertainty.
findings.mitigation: Replace the state parameter with an employer-signed custodial-eligible bucket. Check that T is in the cached set before verifying a proof, and rate-limit. Have counsel confirm that a stored verified proof plus its spentKey satisfies the NC recommendation.

relationship_actually_hidden_from: Employer / HR Tool: it is never involved and learns no wallet, holder, ticket or pickup. It already knows family composition and dates of birth from its own roster, and the design adds nothing to that.
Prescriber: it learns only W_C and what it physically sees in the room. It never learns the guardian, the grandparent, the ticket set or who picks up.

Insurer, engine and sequencer, as to the second-degree holder (grandparent, neighbour) and any relationship label. Salted per-prescription tickets mean no holder identity, kinship code or family edge to the holder ever reaches the network.
Pharmacy records and dashboard, as to the relationship label and the intermediary for a phone-based pickup of a drug that is not controlled. The proof shows only 'authorised for this prescription'.
Network observers, as to the label: it is never on the wire. Timing and IP are covered under the leaks.
relationship_leaks_to: Engine and sequencer, including replica logs: the parent-to-child custodial edge and sibling sets. Custodial wallets ride the parent's member node: node-signed l2_registerEntity, a node-signed /events subscription, the same IP and process, and burst timing. Add the custodialUntil minor bit and the B8 family binding, and roles become inferable. The engine also sees that a second hop exists whenever a transfer rotates a slot, and it sees revocation patterns.

Pharmacy: physical observation (the age gap at the counter). Tier R cards carry a static cardId and a clear rxRef, and the PIN typed on its keypad decrypts every ticket on the card, which links siblings and repeat pickers. It sees same-holder uploads from one IP and two children's bags collected together. For controlled substances, the picker's driving licence plus the patient's PAT data (surname, address, age gap) reveal the relationship, and the NJ/WI rule forces it to learn whether the picker is the patient.
State PDMP, for controlled substances: the picker's ID fields plus the patient's PAT segment, which allow the same surname, address and age inference.

Insurer: family composition through B8 family-history. If it is the verifier, it also sees POA, guardianship, emancipation and custody-change paperwork tied to a wallet. It can tie PICKUP events, and the tier used, to prescriptions it already knows.

Custodial parent: sees which holder collected (by design). Sees that the minor's confidential fills exist, and their amounts, through wallet-update reasons, accumulator moves and any unfiltered route or /nfc/scan history. A policyholder who captures an adult dependent's code sees everything sent to that wallet.

Anyone who finds or skims a Tier R card: the PIN falls to offline brute force against the v2 scrypt/AES-GCM format, giving bearer pickup, and rxRef ties the card to W_C's prescription in the audit chain.

Sequencer replicas and audit-chain readers: the drug, and whether the prescription is confidential, by dictionary attack on rxBinding, because rxId is a low-entropy RX-<ms>-<4 base36> string and PrescriptionData is unsalted.
attack.o1js_feasibility:
Feasible in o1js 2.13, with one strong recommendation to drop the phone-side proof.

The circuits:
- PickupProgram.claim is about 150 rows: three Poseidon hashes, a Provable.if and a five-field Struct public input, with maxProofsVerified 0 and no recursion.
- PickupProgram.transfer is about 200 rows.
- CustodyProgram is one 7-input Poseidon over the member preimage plus a range compare. dob enters as Field(CCYYMMDD) inside hashIdentityDate (src/zkp/hash-utils.ts:124), so it is implementable.

None of these proofs binds to sequencer or ledger roots, so the A-33 staleness problem and the D7/D8 proving lease do not apply to them. The dispense finalize (/interactive/fill) still proves under the lease, so the counter wait is unchanged. Verification with verify(proof, pinnedVk) at the pharmacy and the engine costs roughly a second.

The unknown is phone proving. Pickles' fixed step-and-wrap overhead dominates a circuit this small, and it has never been measured on a handset. o1js needs WASM threads (SharedArrayBuffer with cross-origin isolation), roughly 1-2 GB peak memory, and compiled or cached prover keys on the device. The 22 KB proof fits neither a QR code nor an NTAG216, and iOS restricts NFC card emulation, so upload or BLE is required. Pre-proving hides the latency but not memory or compatibility failures on older phones.

Replacing Tier Z with one-time prekeys removes all of this: H(pk_i) goes in the ticket, and the counter checks an Ed25519 challenge signature. Privacy and holder binding stay the same, with no circuit at all. o1js would then be needed only if CustodyProgram is kept, and an employer-signed custodial bucket could replace it too.

As written, the claim circuit cannot enforce singleFill, because policy is a private input. It needs a public flag or a per-ticket nullifier output.
attack.verdict:
The design answers the owner's question correctly. You never identify a second-degree relationship. Instead you prove authority for one prescription, rooted in the dependent's own wallet, which matches 45 CFR 164.510(b) and 164.502(g). The salted per-prescription ticket genuinely hides the grandparent and any relationship label from the engine, sequencer, insurer, employer and prescriber. It needs no kinship data, and its proofs avoid A-33 because they bind to no ledger root.

The write-up overclaims in five places that must be fixed before building:
1. The intermediary is not hidden from the engine or sequencer. Custodial wallets share the parent's node key, IP and timing, which exposes the parent-to-child and sibling graph.
2. Custody rests on a self-typed date of birth, so a policyholder can capture an adult dependent or a spouse. The handover at majority and co-parent revocation are both controlled by whoever holds the shared key.
3. Tier R reuses the v2 PIN-encrypted card format that PRD-1 retired, so it can be brute-forced offline. Its cardId and rxRef link pickups and siblings, and the PIN typed at the pharmacy decrypts every ticket on the card.
4. The confidential-minor path leaks to the custodial parent through wallet updates, accumulators and routes keyed to W_C. Its prescriber attestation and printed slip together form a fraud channel hidden from parents.
5. The single-fill bit and Tier R refill reuse are not enforced, and pharmacies trust ticket sets served by the engine without checking the controller's signature, so an insider can inject tickets.

Also needed:
- a synchronous revocation check before handover;
- a scoped issuing subkey, because automatic registration fails while the key is locked, and the controller-unavailable case is exactly the grandparent scenario;
- a single issuing device per dependent;
- blind attestation if the insurer verifies paperwork.

For controlled substances, the PDMP and ID rules make the relationship inferable from the records, which justifies keeping them out of release one. Replacing Tier Z with one-time prekeys gives the same privacy with no phone proving.

With these changes the core survives.
